title: Additive combinatorics: the set of C-form certificates for fixed p as a 'multiplicative energy' problem on divisors of {4Cp+1}_C
connection: Writing 4Cp + 1 = ab with a + 1 ≡ b + 1 ≡ 0 (mod 4C): the condition says 4C | gcd(a+1, b+1) and 4C = (ab − 1)/p. So C-form certificates ⟺ pairs (a, b) with (ab − 1)/p dividing both a + 1 and b + 1, and ab ≡ 1 mod p. The set {(a,b): ab ≡ 1 mod p} is the modular hyperbola; we need points on it where the 'height' (ab−1)/p divides a + 1. For a, b ≤ p this forces (ab − 1)/p < p; so it's a question about the modular hyperbola's small-height points with a divisibility — a sum-product-flavoured condition.
why: Sum-product/energy methods (Bourgain–Garaev on modular hyperbolas, Shkredov) give nontrivial pointwise-in-p bounds for incidence-type counts on the hyperbola; they could show the count of (a, b) with the divisibility is ≫ 1 for all p? Unlikely (counts are small) but the hyperbola geometry is the right home for 'why 409 fails'.
first_step: Plot, for p = 409 and a control prime 401, the points (a, b) with ab ≡ 1 mod p, a, b < 4p, colouring those with (ab − 1)/p | gcd(a+1, b+1); see the structural difference.

title: Count the C-form exceptional primes up to X: density → 0 like 1/(log X)^α? or positive density?
connection: If exceptions have positive relative density among primes ≡ 1 mod 24, the C-form is a 'weak' sufficient condition; if they thin out as a power of log, they are the 'tail' and their rate is a measurable analogue of exceptional-set exponents (Vaughan's bound in miniature).
why: Quantifies the gap between C-form and ES; also a test of the 'half-dimensional sieve' heuristics (prediction: exceptions ~ X/(log X)^{1+κ} for the effective sieve dimension κ).
first_step: From the census, fit #exceptions ≤ X vs X/(log X)^β; report β.

title: Mechanism design: an identity family indexed by the Gaussian factorisation p = u² + v² (not polynomial in p but polynomial in (u, v))
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in p on square classes; identities polynomial in (u, v) with p = u² + v² are a different class (p is a quadratic form in the parameters). E.g. try: 4/(u² + v²) = 1/x(u,v) + 1/y(u,v) + 1/z(u,v) with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[u, v] — a polynomial identity in TWO variables over the quadric. Schinzel's theorem is about one variable n; a two-variable identity covering all (u, v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 is not obviously excluded (but a polynomial identity in (u,v) specialises to a polynomial identity in n on... no — n = u² + v² does not make x(u,v) a polynomial in n). Also allowed: identities depending on (u, v) mod small moduli.
why: A genuinely different identity class that respects T1 automatically? (Odd squares m² = u² + v² with... m² = (m)² + 0² or other representations; identities valid only for v ≠ 0 or for gcd(u,v) = 1 would exclude the trivial representation — promising sign.) Search space is small; cheap to run.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁷ compute (a,b) and fit low-degree polynomial forms to the smallest solutions' denominators; check B1 Thm M's scope for procedures that use the two-squares decomposition.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0275] Enumerate candidate x, y, z as low-degree polynomials in (u, v) (degree ≤ 4, small coefficients) satisfying 4xyz = (u²+v²)(xy+yz+zx) identically — polynomial system; solve with Gröbner/ansatz; also allow residue-class branching on (u, v) mod 2, 3, 4.
[upgrades-0232] Search low-degree X, Y, Z ∈ ℚ[a,b] with 4XYZ = (a²+b²)(XY+YZ+ZX) identically and X,Y,Z positive integral on a congruence region; check behaviour at Pythagorean points.

title: Analogy of analogy: T1 ↔ 'Pythagorean loophole' ↔ Hilbert's irreducibility — identities fail exactly where the parameter polynomial takes square values; so ES's obstruction is the square-value locus of EVERY parametrisation
connection: Generalising the previous item: for any parametrisation p = P(t₁, …, t_k) (P a polynomial), a polynomial identity would produce solutions at all values P(t) including those that are odd squares; T1 forbids this; so no polynomial identity exists over any parametrisation P whose value set contains odd squares. Only parametrisations whose value set avoids squares (e.g. P(t) = t² + 1, never a square for t ≥ 1; P = 4t² + 1 never a square for t ≥ 1!) escape. So: polynomial identities for ES along p = 4t² + 1 (or t² + 1, t⁴ + 1…) are NOT excluded by T1 — and primes of the form 4t² + 1 are conjecturally infinite (Landau's 4th problem for t²+1).
why: Identifies a precise loophole class: identities in t for n = 4t² + 1 (or similar square-avoiding polynomials) — a 'conditional infinite family of hard primes' if found (hard class? 4t² + 1 mod 840 can be in square classes: need 4t² + 1 ≡ square mod 840 for some t ✓ possible). Mordell–Schinzel applies to identities in n, not in t with n = 4t² + 1 — check Schinzel's theorem's exact scope (it might cover 'polynomial in t with n polynomial in t').
first_step: Search for polynomial x(t), y(t), z(t) with 4/(4t² + 1) = Σ 1/x_i(t); e.g. try the e-slice/Type II structure: 4C(4t² + 1) + 1 = 16Ct² + 4C + 1 — for C = 1: 16t² + 5 — factor? no; find C(t) polynomial making 4C(t)(4t² + 1) + 1 factor with the right residues. Then read Schinzel 2000 to see whether this is excluded.

title: Check whether Type II with c ≥ 2 is itself just the C-form for a *composite* n: ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 (mod 4cd) ⟺ C-form certificate for n = cp with C = cd?
connection: C-form for n' = cp with C' = cd: 4C'n' + 1 = 4cd·cp + 1 = 4c²dp + 1 ✓ and a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C' = 4cd ✓. So Type II for p with parameters (c, d) is EXACTLY the C-form for the multiple n = cp with parameter C = cd. Hence: ES(p) via Type II ⟺ some multiple cp of p has a C-form certificate; and a solution for cp gives one for p by scaling?? NO — scaling goes the other way (solution for n gives one for multiples). Hmm: C-form for cp gives 4/(cp) = 1/(C'uv) + 1/(cpC'v) + 1/(cpC'u) ⟹ multiply by c: 4/p = c/(C'uv) + 1/(pC'v) + 1/(pC'u) — first term c/(cd·uv) = 1/(duv) ✓ a unit fraction! So yes: a C-form certificate for cp with C' = cd yields 4/p = 1/(duv) + 1/(pcdv) + 1/(pcdu). Consistent. So full Type II ⟺ 'some multiple cp of p, with C a multiple of c, has a C-form certificate' — the slack is exactly 'pass to a multiple'.
why: Clean structural dictionary: the C-form is the 'primitive' statement and Type II is its closure under passing to multiples cp with C ∈ cℤ. For 409: n = 818, C = 2 works. So the C-form exceptional set E and ES relate by: ES(p) ⟺ ∃c: (cp, C ∈ cℤ)-C-form certificate. The 'C-form conjecture for all non-square n' (if true) would imply ES immediately (take c = 1); its failure at 409 shows the conjecture is false for primes — so the right C-form conjecture is 'for every n, some multiple cn has a C-form certificate with c | C' — which is just ES.
first_step: Record the dictionary; recompute: for each C-form exception p, the smallest c such that cp has a C-form certificate with c | C (409: c=2).

title: Is the e-slice form ('∃ e ≡ −p mod 4 with −1 ∈ {ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}') the right 'primitive' with no exceptions? Compute its exceptional set vs C-form's
connection: The repo's e-slice form is stated as ⟺ ES(p) (FRONTIER §1), with N = (p+e)/4 (Type II) or (pe+1)/4 (Type I). Unlike the C-form it is claimed equivalent; its one-parameter nature (e) vs the C-form's suggests the e-slice packs (c, d) into e. Verify the equivalence numerically and compute the smallest winning e for the exceptions 409, 577, …
why: Establishes which one-parameter form is exact; informs the 'dimension' items.
first_step: Implement the e-slice test; verify against brute-force ES for p ≤ 3000; report e_min for the four exceptional primes.

title: Finite differences in C: Δ_C of the indicator win(p, C) — is the sequence C ↦ win(p, C) 'eventually periodic' or 'quasi-periodic' for fixed p?
connection: For fixed p the C-form win indicator depends on the factorisation of the linear sequence 4Cp+1 — a shifted-prime-factor structure with no periodicity but with 'almost periodicity' in the Besicovitch sense (periodic in C mod q for each small prime q's contribution).
why: If win(p, ·) is Besicovitch almost periodic with a positive mean for every p, then infinitely many C win — pointwise ES with infinitude; the mean's positivity is the question, again — but almost-periodicity theory (Wintner, Schwarz–Spilker) gives a *formula* for the mean as a sum over 'Ramanujan expansions', which might be analysable.
first_step: Compute the Ramanujan–Fourier coefficients of win(p, C) over C ≤ 10⁵ for a few p; check whether the mean (the C-density of winning C) is approximated by the first few terms and is bounded away from 0 across p.

title: Umbral / generating-function identities for the count Σ_C x^C·#{a | 4Cp+1, a ≡ −1 (4C)}: Lambert-series structure
connection: Σ_N τ(N) x^N is a Lambert series; sums restricted to N = 4Cp+1 and a in a class tied to C are 'twisted Lambert series along an AP with varying modulus'. Lambert series have modular transformation properties; perhaps the C-form generating function has a transformation law relating p and 1/p-ish parameters.
why: A transformation law would be a rigid analytic structure (like Zagier's for Σ H(n)q^n). Low-to-medium prior.
first_step: Compute the generating function numerically for small p at |x| < 1 and test for simple transformation behaviour under x → e^{−2πt} ↦ t → 1/(p t)-type substitutions.

title: Wythoff/Fibonacci game lens: the pair (a, b) with ab = 4Cp+1, a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C satisfies (a+1)(b+1) = 4C(p + u + v)…: write the Diophantine system as a lattice-point problem in the (u, v) plane under a hyperbola and count by Dirichlet's hyperbola method
connection: p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟺ (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1: for fixed C, solutions (u, v) are lattice points on a hyperbola; summing over C ≤ X, the total count is a 'hyperbola-method' sum Σ_C #{(u,v)}; Dirichlet's method gives main terms with error terms — standard for Σ_{C} τ(4Cp+1) — but here the hyperbola is in (u, v) with the constraint built in. Just the Type II count in the (u,v) coordinates: Σ_{C ≤ X} #{u ≤ v : (4Cu − 1) | 4Cp+1}.
why: A clean reparametrisation: the C-form ⟺ ∃ u ≥ 1: p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u). This is the same shape (tied modulus) but with the *additive* shift p + u instead of the multiplicative 4Cp + 1 — i.e., the e-slice form with e = u (N = (p + e)/4-ish). It makes the role of u symmetric with v and shows the C-form is a statement about the divisors of p + 1, p + 2, p + 3, … in classes −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …: 'the shifted primes p + u, u = 1, 2, 3, …, cannot ALL avoid divisors ≡ −1 mod 4u'. Verify and record; this is probably the repo's e-slice form in disguise (seen).
first_step: Verify algebraically and numerically: C-form certificate ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) [with the cofactor condition automatically satisfied?]. Then for p = 409: p + u for u ≤ 60000 never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u?! Check directly — this gives a very concrete statement about 409: '410, 411, 412, … have no divisor ≡ −1 mod 4, 8, 12, …' — e.g. 410 = 2·5·41: divisors ≡ 3 mod 4: none (5, 41 ≡ 1; 2·5 = 10 ≡ 2; …) ✓; 411 = 3·137: need ≡ 7 mod 8: 3, 137 ≡ 1, 411 ≡ 3 — none ✓; 412 = 4·103: need ≡ 11 mod 12: 103 ≡ 7, 206 ≡ 2, 412 ≡ 4 — none ✓ … So 409 is a prime such that p + u never has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u. A beautiful concrete puzzle.

title: Hasse-principle-style 'almost local' obstruction for 409 in the shifted form: is there a modulus M such that for every u the condition 'p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u' is blocked by p's residue mod M? (A 'uniform local obstruction' — would contradict the belief that only squares are obstructed)
connection: For a fixed u the condition on p is a union of residue classes mod lcm-ish(4u·a); an obstruction for ALL u from a single residue p mod M would mean the C-form fails on an entire AP of primes — plausibly false (Dirichlet + the almost-all results for the C-form). So 409's failure is not an AP obstruction; is it then 'random' (and the C ≤ 60000 search just unlucky — implausible given the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409C+1)/φ(4C) ≈ 52 wins) or a non-AP structural obstruction (like T1, which is a 'square' obstruction — not an AP either)? Expected 66 wins vs 0 observed strongly indicates an obstruction of a new type (not AP, not square).
why: The expected-count argument (≈ 52 expected certificates for 409 with C ≤ 60000 (computed: Σ τ(4·409·C+1)/φ(4C) = 51.8), zero observed) is the sharpest evidence that 409 is structurally obstructed in the C-form; identifying the obstruction type is a genuinely new piece of ES structure.
first_step: Compute the expected count Σ_{C ≤ 60000} τ(4·409·C + 1)/φ(4C) precisely (it is the natural heuristic) and compare with the 0 observed; then test the natural candidate obstruction: for 409, is the forced QNR condition (a/409) = −1 incompatible with a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) and a | 4·409C + 1 for a reason involving 409 ≡ 9 (mod 16) or 409's Gaussian representation 20² + 3²?

title: Shifted form for composite n and the T1 reproof: m² + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u) is impossible — one-line check via (a/m²) = 1
connection: For n = m²: a | m² + u, a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (a/m²) = 1 but the forced symbol says (a/n) = −1 — contradiction. T1 for the C-form in the shifted language is immediate. For general n the forced symbol is (a/n) = −1 (Jacobi), which for n = 409·k² etc. reduces to (a/409) = −1 — so the shifted-form exceptional set is closed under multiplication by odd squares coprime to… (need also a | n + u to be consistent) — test numerically whether 409·9 is an exception.
why: Closure under square multiples would give an infinite non-square family of C-form exceptions (409m²), making the C-form exceptional set 'squares ∪ square-multiples of sporadic ∪ ?' — a rich structure to compare with the U(n) sporadics {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145} (are these square multiples of smaller ones? 2961 = 9·329 = 9·7·47; 25305 = 105·241; hmm).
first_step: Compute the C-form exceptional set for n ≤ 10⁵ (all n ≡ 1 mod 4, u ≤ 5000) and test closure under n ↦ nm²; compare to the U(n) list.

title: Non-congruence classes: polynomial identities valid on Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields (e.g. 2 a quartic residue)
connection: Mordell–Schinzel rule out polynomial identities on square classes (congruence classes). Classes like 'p = x² + 64y²' (2 is a quartic residue) are Chebotarev classes of non-abelian fields and are not unions of congruence classes, so identities with p-dependent algebraic parameters (e.g. involving x, y with p = x² + 64y²) could cover them.
why: The repo has NONCONG_LIFTS. Native class-field-theory classes give an infinite supply of new 'families' whose parameters are norms (x,y), sidestepping the congruence-class formulation of B1.
first_step: Search for ES identities in parameters (x, y) with p = x² + y² (or x² + 64y²) of bounded degree, e.g. x = f(a,b) with p = a² + b², by polynomial ansatz + solve; test coverage of the hard class.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0098] For p ≡ 1 mod 840, test whether p = N(α) for α in ℤ[ζ_3, 2^{1/3}] (i.e. p = x³-form represented) gives a uniform certificate formula.

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli factorisation as divisor-structure input
connection: Norms of differences of singular moduli have explicitly known prime factorisations (all primes ≤ D1D2/4) ↔ ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in a class.
why: An integer tied to p with explicitly controlled factorisation (only small primes, with Legendre-symbol constraints) is exactly what the 'class gate' wants.
first_step: Compute N(j(τ_{−4p}) − j(τ_{−3}))-type quantities for small p and check if they produce divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1-type integers.

title: Lucas-sequence primitive divisors (Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier) as a source of prime divisors ≡ −1 (mod m)
connection: Primitive prime divisors q of U_m(P,Q) satisfy q ≡ (D/q) (mod m), so q ≡ −1 (mod m) when (D/q) = −1. ES Type II needs a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of 4Cp+1. If 4Cp+1 shares a primitive divisor with a suitable U_{4C}, the certificate follows.
why: BHV give existence of primitive divisors for all m > 30, a pointwise rigidity theorem. The question is whether p-dependent Lucas sequences can be tied to 4Cp+1.
first_step: Find a Lucas sequence u_m(p) with index m ~ 4C such that p-tied integers 4Cp+1 contain u_m's primitive divisor; test small cases.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0196] Look for Lucas parameters (P,Q) depending on p with 4Cp+1 | U_{4C}(P,Q)·(small) for some C; test small p by search.

[upgrades-0080] For small D and n = 4C, list primitive divisors q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) of u_n and test how often p + m ≡ 0 (mod q) can be arranged (it cannot for fixed p unless q | p + m; compute the induced density).
refs: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (Crelle 2001)

title: Abc conjecture consequences for ES failures
connection: ABC controls radicals ↔ an ES counterexample p forces all 4Cp+1 (C ≤ polylog) to avoid divisors in −1 mod 4C; does that force smoothness/radical patterns contradicting abc?
why: Implications from abc to Diophantine non-existence are standard; here we want abc ⟹ existence, which is unusual but possible via 'no huge prime-power structure' arguments.
first_step: Check whether the failure of (★) for p forces 4Cp+1 to be prime or a prime power for many C — and whether that's restricted by known results (it isn't by abc; record negative).

title: Harmonic-mean interpretation: p/4·3 is the harmonic mean of x,y,z
connection: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ harmonic mean H(x,y,z) = 3p/4 ↔ means inequalities (H ≤ G ≤ A) give box constraints.
why: Box constraints from mean inequalities are already used; the 'harmonic mean of three integers equals 3p/4' phrasing might connect to integer means literature.
first_step: Search 'integers with prescribed harmonic mean' literature for existence theorems.

title: Dual certificates of failure: what does a 'proof of no Type II (★) solution' look like for p = 409?
connection: Each (★)-failing prime has a finite proof of failure (exhaustion) ↔ shortest such proof structure (via sieving modulo few primes?) reveals what a counterexample to ES would require.
why: If (★)-failures always have short structured proofs (e.g. via a few congruences), then ES-failure needs a similar compact obstruction pattern, which might be ruled out.
first_step: For the 14 (★)-failing primes, compute the minimal set of residue checks proving failure (it's a covering of the trial set); look for common shape.

title: Gröbner/elimination for identity families: Mordell–Schinzel boundary computed
connection: Elimination theory can compute all polynomial identity families of bounded degree for 4/n (sections of the ES fibration of degree ≤ d over ℚ[t]).
why: Exhaustive classification of low-degree families tells exactly which classes polynomial identities can reach.
first_step: Set up unknown-coefficient polynomials x(t), y(t), z(t), n(t) of degree ≤ 3 and solve the coefficient system with Gröbner bases (msolve/Singular).
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0206] Set up unknown-coefficient degree-2 polynomials x(t),y(t),z(t),n(t) and solve the identity via Gröbner; list families and their n-images.
refs: Schinzel, On sums of three unit fractions with polynomial denominators, Funct. Approx. 28 (2000)

title: Smooth values of 4Cp+1: certificate abundance when some level is smooth
connection: If 4Cp + 1 has many prime factors whose classes in (ℤ/4C)^× are in general position (smoothness alone is not enough: factors all ≡ 1 mod 4 never give a level-4 certificate), its divisors cover (ℤ/4C)^× (subset products), so a certificate exists. ES would follow from 'for every p some C ≤ (log p)^A has 4Cp + 1 with ≥ k prime factors in general position'.
why: Smooth-number theory (Canfield–Erdős–Pomerance; smooth values of linear forms, Harman; Balog–Wooley) gives existence of smooth values in short families. One value with many factors is a pointwise target with a native toolbox.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes, min over C ≤ 10⁴ of the largest prime factor of 4Cp+1 relative to the requirement Ω ≥ D((ℤ/4C)^×) ; record gap.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0244] Find the best known result on 'some n ≤ N^ε in a linear family an + b has a smooth or many-factor value' (Balog, Harman), and compare the family length (log p)^A with what is needed.
refs: Granville, Smooth numbers: computational number theory and beyond (2008)

title: Dirichlet hyperbola method for R(p) with exact error tracking
connection: R(p) = Σ_C #{d | 4Cp+1 : d ≡ −1 mod 4C} ↔ split d ≤ √ and d > √; symmetry d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d preserves class (since product ≡ 1 mod 4C ⇒ cofactor ≡ −1).
why: Already used (R even). Exploit further: the pairing is an involution with no fixed points (squares excluded) — parity of half-count R/2 has no forced value (EVIDENCE fair coin). Record as done.
first_step: Check whether a refined involution (e.g. using d ↔ (4C'p+1)/d across different C) produces a fixed-point-only-at-squares structure.

title: When 4Cp+1 is prime, the C-slice of (★) fails; when is 4Cp+1 = q·r with q ≡ −1 mod 4C?
connection: Prime 4Cp+1 kills slice C; semiprimes succeed iff a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C ↔ quadratic-character-like conditions on factors.
why: Breaking R(p) by factorisation type of 4Cp+1 gives a clean probabilistic model: success probability of slice C ≈ Σ over factorisation types.
first_step: Tabulate, over C ≤ 100 and p ≤ 10⁶, the success rate of slice C conditioned on Ω(4Cp+1) = 2, 3, 4…

title: Prime-modulus certificate family as a covering-by-primes question (Erdős covering with prime moduli)
connection: From previous: ES ⟸ p ∈ ∪_ℓ ∪_{C | (ℓ+1)/4} {−(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ} ↔ covering the primes by residue classes mod distinct primes ℓ with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes each.
why: Covering systems with distinct prime moduli cannot cover ℤ when Σ (#classes)/ℓ converges or by Hough-type results; here Σ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ diverges — so covering is not excluded by density; but CRT construction evades finite subsets (B1).
first_step: Formalise 'prime-modulus covering with τ((ℓ+1)/4) classes per ℓ' and check whether known results (Erdős, Simpson–Zeilberger on coverings with prime moduli?) exclude covering all integers (likely yes via CRT) — then all primes is a different question (record).

title: Multiplicative energy of the divisor set of 4Cp+1
connection: Additive/multiplicative energy of divisor sets ↔ structured sets cover subgroups faster.
why: Divisor sets have maximal multiplicative structure (they're 'cubes' {Π p_i^{e_i}}); covering results for 'generalised geometric progressions' in (ℤ/q)^× are precise.
first_step: Model divisors as a generalised GP with k generators; compute the minimal k for which such sets cover −1 mod q generically; compare with Ω(4Cp+1).

title: Identities in terms of sum-of-two-squares representation p = a² + b²
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 is a² + b² ↔ search for x,y,z polynomial in (a,b) with 4/(a²+b²) = 1/x+1/y+1/z holding identically or on an explicit infinite set.
why: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities in n on residue classes containing squares, but identities in (a,b) are a different object: n = a²+b² is a polynomial in two variables. Does the obstruction persist? (Probably yes via specialisation b=0 giving squares a² — T1 obstruction! then need identities that avoid b = 0 ... record.)
first_step: Check: any identity in (a,b) specialises at b=0 to n = a² (odd square) where Type I/II solutions don't exist (T1) — so any (a,b)-identity must produce non-Type-I/II or fail at b = 0 — test whether rational functions with a pole at b = 0 escape this.

title: Identities with poles at the T1 locus: rational (not polynomial) parametrisations x(a,b) with denominators vanishing on b = 0
connection: Following the T1 specialisation obstruction: any (a,b)-identity must break at squares; rational functions with b in denominators break exactly there.
why: Integrality then requires b | numerators — a divisibility condition in (a,b) that may hold for all p via a choice among the many representations a² + b² (only one up to sign for primes!) — so only finitely many choices; record as likely-dead but clean test.
first_step: Search rational functions of low degree in (a,b) with denominators b^k for identities 4/(a²+b²) = Σ 1/x_i; then test integrality on primes.

title: Sterile points as profinite objects: x** in Ẑ where all ET identities fail
connection: A sterile point is a profinite integer (point of Ẑ) where no ET identity class contains it ↔ compactness: if no sterile prime-like points exist in the closure of primes in Ẑ, ES would follow from finitely many identities — contradicting B1 — so sterile points must exist; their structure is the obstruction.
why: Classifying sterile profinite points (are they all squares in Ẑ? i.e. locally squares everywhere) would connect B1 to T1: sterile ⟺ 'locally a square' would be a clean theorem.
first_step: Test: are all known sterile points squares in ℤ_ℓ for every ℓ checked? Compute for x** its square-class in ℤ_ℓ for ℓ ≤ 50.

title: Shifted-square obstruction: why squares fail Type I/II via Jacobi symbols, and 'almost squares' (p = m² + small) as stress tests
connection: T1 kills odd squares; primes p = m² + k for small k are 'close to squares' ↔ maybe low certificate counts for small k.
why: If R(m² + k)/M is systematically small for small k, T1's influence leaks to neighbours — a quantitative T1 continuity phenomenon to explain or exploit.
first_step: Compute R(p)/M_BM(p) for primes p = m² + k, k ∈ {4, 16, 36, …} (to keep p ≡ 1 mod 4) vs random p; m ≤ 10⁴.

title: Sum over t of #{d | tp+1, d ≡ −1 mod t}: the full I3 count as a thick object with t up to p
connection: Allowing t up to ~p gives a sum of ~p log p events; for t > √p, the divisor condition is about tp+1 having a divisor in a class mod t > √(tp) — Lenstra regime (≤ bounded count, decidable fast).
why: In the large-t regime, the condition d ≡ −1 mod t with d | tp+1 forces d small multiple structure: d = kt − 1 with (kt−1) | tp+1 ⟺ (kt−1) | (p + k)·t − (kt−1)·… ⟹ (kt − 1) | p + k: back to Type II trial form. Symmetry u ↔ k — consistent.
first_step: Map the I3 large-t regime onto small-k Type II trials explicitly; confirm the count identity numerically.

title: Polynomial ES over ℤ[T] (not F_q[T]): 4/f(T) = Σ 1/g_i(T) and specialisation
connection: Solutions in ℤ[T] for polynomial n(T) give identity families ↔ Mordell–Schinzel classification.
why: Systematic: for each polynomial n(T) of degree ≤ 2, decide existence of ℤ[T] solutions; the set of n(T) admitting them maps to proved thin families.
first_step: Enumerate quadratic n(T) = aT² + bT + c with small coefficients and search ℤ[T] solutions with degree ≤ 4 denominators.

title: Small-q pieces: B = q small ⟹ condition u | p + B with u ≡ −p mod B, i.e. divisors of p+1, p+2, … in classes
connection: For small B the C-equation reads: p + B has a divisor u ≡ … Actually p + B = u(4BC − 1) ⟹ the cofactor 4BC − 1 ≡ −1 mod 4B divides p + B ↔ the shift form at small B.
why: Small-B slices are 'divisors of p+B for B ≤ K in class −1 mod 4B': these are K concrete integers next to p. The union over B ≤ K gives a fixed menu (B1 applies), but how fast does coverage grow with K?
first_step: Compute fraction of primes ≤ 10⁸ covered by B ≤ K slices for K = 1..100; fit coverage curve.

title: Cubic polynomial T²(T − s) + e(T − n/4) with three positive integer roots
connection: x,y,z are the roots of T³ − sT² + e₂T − e₃ with 4e₃ = n·e₂, i.e. of 4T²(T−s) + e₂(4T − n). So ES(n) ⇔ for some (s, e₂) this cubic splits completely over ℤ with positive roots.
why: It is a 'totally split specialisation' problem for a 2-parameter family of cubics. Hilbert-irreducibility counting and 'polynomials with many split values' (Schinzel-type) are the native field.
first_step: Compute the Galois group over Q(s,e) (generic S₃) and the discriminant surface. Check whether split points lie on a subvariety with a parametrisation (they should be exactly U_n).
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0354] Check the gcd bookkeeping (e₂ divisible by 4 when n odd?), then compute the discriminant of the family as a polynomial in (a,j,n) and test whether 'discriminant is a square' is a tractable curve condition.

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the trial indicator: 1[m | N] = (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(N)
connection: R(p) = Σ_{(u,C)} (1/m) Σ_{d|m} c_d(p+u) with m = 4uC−1 ↔ Ramanujan–Fourier expansion separates main term (d = 1) and oscillation (Ramanujan sums c_d(p+u)).
why: Ramanujan sums are explicit; regrouping by d gives R(p) = Σ_d (Σ_{m ≡ 0 (d)} …) c_d(·) — possibly revealing a d-level where cancellation fails exactly at squares (T1).
first_step: Compute the contribution of each d ≤ 100 to R(p) for hard p and for odd squares; see which d carry the T1 cancellation.

title: Type I / Type II complementarity: are the primes where Type II is scarce rich in Type I?
connection: f_I(p) and f_II(p) counts ↔ correlation across primes.
why: Negative correlation would suggest a conservation-type law (a combined invariant), positive correlation suggests common difficulty driver (local factors).
first_step: Compute Spearman correlation of f_I(p)/log³p and f_II(p)/log³p over primes ≤ 10⁷ (repo data) after removing local-factor main terms.

title: Divisors ≡ −1 mod m of numbers ≡ 1 mod m: forced when the number has a 'twisted' structure (e.g. N = a² − b² with a ≡ 0, b ≡ 1?)
connection: If N = (A − 1)(A + 1)/k-type factorisations with A ≡ 0 mod m, then A − 1 ≡ −1 mod m is a divisor ↔ ES: 4Cp+1 = (A−1)(A+1)/… would need 4Cp + 1 + 1 = A²·… hmm: 4Cp+1 = d·d' with d ≡ d' ≡ −1 mod 4C; d = A − 1, d' = A' − 1.
why: Clarifies: ES Type II ⟺ 4Cp+1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1); writing as difference of squares, 4Cp+1 = ((d+d')/2)² − ((d−d')/2)² — a representation as difference of squares with constraints mod 4C on the sum — a quadratic-form representation question.
first_step: Rewrite ES Type II as: 4Cp + 1 = X² − Y² with X ≡ −1 (mod 4C)... (X = (d+d')/2 ≡ −1 mod 2C) and test whether this binary-quadratic view yields anything beyond divisor form.

title: Cunningham-chain-like structures: p with 4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1, … all prime or class-constrained
connection: Simultaneous primality of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ K (Dickson-type tuple) ↔ the B1 construction of hard primes.
why: Searching for primes with long runs of prime 4Cp+1 gives naturally hard test cases for (★) (not for ES itself).
first_step: Search p ≤ 10¹² for the longest run C = 1..K with every 4Cp+1 prime; compute R(p) and full ES count for the record holders.

title: Hypothesis-H-generated hard primes vs ES: do they also stress Type I?
connection: Dickson-tuple primes kill small (★) slices but Type I slices (divisors of p² + 4c²d) are different ↔ test whether Type I compensates.
why: If Type I is uncorrelated with the tuple construction, ES's union is robust to single-family adversaries — evidence on the 'independent families' model.
first_step: For the record primes from the previous item compute f_I(p) and compare with typical p.

title: Self-similarity: does R(p) for p in the hardest classes look like R of smaller primes rescaled (renormalisation in modulus)?
connection: Compare the distribution of R(p)/M(p) within p ≡ 1 mod 840 with that within p ≡ 1 mod 840·k for growing k ↔ scale-invariance of difficulty.
why: If deeper residue restriction keeps reducing R/M without bound, extremely structured primes could be dangerous (quantifies B1 drift); if it saturates, ES is robust.
first_step: Compute mean R/M over primes ≤ 10⁸ in nested classes p ≡ 1 mod 840, 840·11, 840·11·13, … (all-QR classes) and plot vs modulus.

title: Restrict ES to its σ₂-level sets: (x,y,z) with xy+yz+zx = M and xyz = nM/4
connection: Every ES solution lies on a pair of level sets of elementary symmetric functions σ₂ = M, σ₃ = nM/4; for each M, (x,y,z) are roots of T³ − σ₁T² + MT − nM/4.
why: Turns ES into: find M and σ₁ such that a cubic with these coefficients splits over ℤ with positive roots — a 'split cubic' problem like those handled by discriminant/class-group methods.
first_step: For hard primes p ≤ 10⁶ list the M = σ₂ values of all solutions; look for structure (e.g. M ≡ 0 mod p, M/p values) suggesting a 1-parameter family.

title: Tenenbaum's divisor concentration / Maier–Tenenbaum propinquity for class-divisors
connection: Maier–Tenenbaum solved Erdős's propinquity problem (most n have two divisors with ratio in (1,2]); ES needs two complementary divisors a,b of N with a ≡ −b (mod e) — 'propinquity in residue classes'.
why: Propinquity-type results (divisors close together) are the multiplicative-interval analogue of ES's residue-class closeness.
first_step: Check whether a residue-class analogue of Maier–Tenenbaum ('almost all N have a divisor ≡ −1 mod q for q ≤ (log N)^c') is in the literature.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0250] Define 'class-propinquity': ∃ a ≠ b, ab | N, a ≡ −b (mod e); compute its frequency for random N vs ES slices.
refs: Maier–Tenenbaum, On the set of divisors of an integer, Invent. Math. 76 (1984)
unverified: Maier, Tenenbaum 1984, On the set of divisors of an integer (Invent. Math.)

title: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier primitive divisors ≡ ±1 mod n supply divisors-in-class for Lucas-type ES families
connection: Primitive prime divisors of the n-th Lucas number u_n satisfy q ≡ (D/q) mod n, and exist for all n > 30 (BHV). That is a guaranteed divisor in a class tied to the index — exactly F10 — for integers in exponential families.
why: The campaign's proved thin families (3·2^s+1, 4^s+105, …) used algebraic factorizations; BHV could give a systematic source of divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C for p-tied integers in Lucas families.
first_step: For the open families 15·2^s+1 and 4^s+297: write 4C·p+1 for small C as a Lucas-sequence value or factor thereof and check whether a primitive divisor lands in the needed class.
refs: unverified: Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier 2001, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Gauss Eureka (n = Δ + Δ + Δ ⟺ 8n + 3 = sum of three odd squares): linear change of variable to a local-global problem
connection: ∀n statement solved by transforming n ↦ 8n + 3 and invoking three squares. ES's divisor forms also transform p ↦ 4Cp + 1, p + 4d (F10).
why: A single fixed affine transformation sufficed there; ES needs a family of transformations (one per C) — the cost of the extra quantifier.
first_step: Look for an ES equivalent with a single affine transform (e.g. a statement about 4p + 1 alone with a richer witness) — e.g. via the Frobenius semigroup item.

title: Divisors in residue classes via sign changes
connection: Lenstra's divisor-in-residue-class algorithm, revisited in arXiv:2410.05030, matches ES F10/F15/F21: a tied integer's divisor in a prescribed residue class is the witness-shaped target.
why: This is the closest direct arithmetic match to ES's divisor reformulation, and the abstract reports an algorithmic method based on a sign change.
first_step: Read the algorithm and try its sign-change sequence on the ES tied integer 4Cp+1 with target divisor residue −1 mod 4C for the smallest C-family.

title: Polynomial identity methods for Diophantine coverings
connection: Polynomial identity problems share F03, F09, F34, F35: finite algebraic families cover some classes but may provably miss others.
why: Their obstruction proofs could sharpen understanding of what an infinite covering must add beyond finite congruences.
first_step: Formalize ES identity families as polynomial maps and compute the algebraic locus they cover modulo several small primes.

title: Multiplication-table divisor distribution
connection: Multiplication tables share F10, F15, F21: ES needs a divisor in a specific congruence class of a tied integer.
why: Fine-scale divisor distribution could improve over generic divisor-count estimates.
first_step: For the forms 4Cp+1, tabulate divisors by residue class and interval for a bounded sample of primes, then compare with known multiplication-table bounds.

title: Covering congruences in prime representation problems
connection: Finite congruence coverings share F03, F29, F34 and build a union of identity families over residue classes.
why: Covering-system optimization might reveal a broader set of usable identities, even if finite coverage is impossible.
first_step: Encode existing ES identity conditions as residue-class sets modulo a common modulus and search for minimal complementary covers.

title: Small-prime-factor witnesses: q | 4Cp + 1 with q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) is itself a witness (d = q)
connection: If a prime q ≡ −1 (mod 4C) divides 4Cp + 1 then the cofactor is ≡ −1 too (product ≡ 1), so d = q is a (★) witness. For each prime q and each C with 4C | q + 1, q | 4Cp + 1 is a single congruence on p mod q.
why: So the set of p witnessed by (q, C) is one residue class mod q; (★)(p) for a hard prime p ⟸ p lies in some class {p ≡ −(4C)⁻¹ mod q : 4C | q+1} — an infinite covering by single residue classes (F34). These are (★) witnesses, so the covering misses the 14 (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰; for ES it must be combined with other lines. Note q ≥ 4C − 1, so q ≈ C scale.
first_step: For each hard prime p ≤ 10⁸, find the least prime q such that some C with 4C | q + 1 satisfies q | 4Cp + 1; study the distribution of that q.

title: Friedlander–Iwaniec asymptotic sieve (x²+y⁴) for thin certificate families
connection: FI breaks parity for primes x²+y⁴ via bilinear forms on a thin quadratic sequence; ES Type I with d a square gives p² + (2cy)², sums of two squares.
why: Restricting to d = y² makes the Type I object a Gaussian norm, where FI-type bilinear technology is designed to work.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10^7, the fraction of primes with an ES Type I certificate having d a perfect square, and whether it stays bounded below.
refs: Friedlander–Iwaniec, The polynomial X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Ann. Math. 148 (1998)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Breuillard–Green–Tao approximate groups for the divisor quotient set
connection: BGT classify approximate groups as near nilpotent cosets; in abelian (ℤ/e)^× this is Freiman–Green–Ruzsa; the ES quotient set Q is a product set.
why: If Q is an approximate group, it is near a coset progression, and −1 ∈ Q becomes an explicit lattice question.
first_step: Test on data whether divisor quotient sets are approximate groups (|Q·Q| ≤ K|Q| for small K).
refs: Breuillard–Green–Tao, The structure of approximate groups, Publ. IHES 116 (2012)

title: Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger uniform Mordell for curves in the ES certificate space
connection: DGH (Annals 2021) bound the number of rational points on genus ≥ 2 curves uniformly in terms of genus and rank; ES auxiliary curves (multiple simultaneous ES conditions) have such genus.
why: Uniform bounds limit how many n can share a structured multi-solution pattern — informative for repeated-certificate statistics.
first_step: Construct the curve 'n has two ES solutions sharing x and y-ratio t' and compute its genus as a function of the constraints.
refs: Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger, Uniformity in Mordell–Lang for curves, Ann. Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:2001.10276

title: OAI 012 joint Dickman law for consecutive integers ↔ consecutive Type II slices
connection: OAI 012 claims log P⁺(n)/log n and log P⁺(n+1)/log n are asymptotically independent (Erdős–Pomerance). At fixed p the Type II slices N_e = (p+e)/4, e = e₀, e₀+4, …, are consecutive integers N, N+1, N+2, …
why: Joint anatomy of consecutive integers is exactly the joint law of successive ES slices at one p; independence-type theorems for consecutive integers are the right genre (though they average over n, here n ≈ p/4 + small).
first_step: Measure, at hard primes, the joint distribution of (ω, P⁺, smoothness) of N, N+1, …, N+K for the first K slices vs random consecutive integers near p/4; read OAI 012's method for short-range uniformity.

title: OAI 021 quadratic Jacobsthal bound (claimed) for slices avoiding bad primes
connection: OAI 021 claims every interval of C·k²/(log log k)² integers contains one coprime to any m with ≤ k prime factors; ES e-slices form an interval of consecutive N_e.
why: Guarantees, within a short window of slices, an N_e coprime to any prescribed bad modulus — e.g. avoiding primes that obstruct (−1 ∉ Q). It forces avoidance, not hitting, but is a pointwise every-interval statement.
first_step: Identify a finite set of 'obstructing primes' for e-slice success at a hard prime and compute whether Jacobsthal-avoidance within the first slices helps.

title: Hasse norm principle / Tate cohomology for ray-class formulations of Type I
connection: Type I as 'an ideal of norm f in a ray class mod 4cd in ℚ(√−d)' invokes norm groups; Hasse's norm theorem (cyclic) gives local–global for norms.
why: Turns part of the Type I condition into class field theory, possibly identifying a reciprocity layer (T1) as a ray-class character.
first_step: Compute the ray class group mod 4cd of ℚ(√−d) and identify the subgroup the Type I condition requires, for small c,d.
refs: Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory (1999), ch. VI

title: Inverse Littlewood–Offord for I3 at fixed t: walks in (ℤ/t)^×
connection: For I3 at fixed t, success needs a divisor of tn+1 ≡ −1 (mod t) — a signed subset-product hitting −1 in (ℤ/t)^× (t small!).
why: Small t means a tiny group: random-walk/local-limit arguments are much stronger than for ES's large e; I3 might be provable where ES isn't, isolating why.
first_step: For n ≤ 10^9 and t ≤ 20, measure the fraction of (n,t) with the event and the dependence across t at fixed n.

title: Maynard–Tao weights over the slice index e at fixed p
connection: At fixed p the slices N_e = (p+e)/4 are consecutive integers; MT weights over admissible tuples of slices could force several slices to be 'structured' (e.g. have a small prime factor in a chosen class) simultaneously.
why: Fixed-p, average over e: legitimate without averaging over p — and MT weights are designed for consecutive-integer tuples.
first_step: Choose an admissible k-tuple of slice offsets and compute (numerically) the MT weighted proportion of windows where ≥ 2 slices succeed.
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Murmuration-type averages of I3 counts against n mod t
connection: Average I3 counts as a function of n's residue pattern across t could show oscillations analogous to murmurations.
why: Exposes hidden structure that residue-class fits might miss.
first_step: Plot normalised I3 counts averaged in windows vs n/X and residues mod 840.

title: Kollár–Shepherd-Barron P-resolutions and Wahl singularities 1/m²(1, ma−1) as the T1 locus
connection: T-singularities 1/(dm²)(1, dma−1) have ℚ-Gorenstein smoothings with Milnor number d − 1; the Wahl case d = 1, i.e. 1/m²(1, ma−1), has rational-homology-disk (QHD) smoothings. These sit at square orders m², exactly where T1 kills certificates. KSB P-resolutions of 1/p(1,A) are counted by zero continued fractions.
why: The T1 obstruction may be the shadow of 'square-order cyclic quotients admit QHD smoothings'. Smoothing theory would then give a geometric reason for the square/prime dichotomy.
first_step: Compute, for A ∈ L₃(m²), whether 1/m²(1,A) is a Wahl singularity or admits a QHD smoothing, and compare with the T1 certificate emptiness.

title: Bhargava cubes: the Type II cube point (c,d,j) as a 2×2×2 integer cube
connection: FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS packages Type II data as a cube point; Bhargava's cube law composes three binary quadratic forms. If certificates are cubes with a fixed corner, composition gives relations among certificates of different n.
why: Bhargava's parametrisations come with orbit-counting (geometry of numbers on prehomogeneous spaces), which gives averages but sometimes also exact class-group relations.
first_step: Write a certificate as an explicit 2×2×2 cube and compute its three binary forms; check which one has discriminant related to p and what composition does to certificates.
refs: Bhargava, Higher composition laws I (Ann. Math. 2004)

title: Kudla Diff-parity and T1: incoherent Eisenstein series derivative as a 'certificate counting function'
connection: KUDLA_ES: T1 ⟺ oddness of Kudla's Diff(T). The derivative of an incoherent Eisenstein series at the centre has Fourier coefficients that are arithmetic degrees of special cycles (Kudla–Rapoport–Yang).
why: If ES certificate counts were arithmetic degrees on a Shimura curve or variety, the arithmetic Siegel–Weil formula would give exact identities, with positivity coming from geometry.
first_step: Check whether certificates of level d correspond to special 0-cycles Z(T) on a quaternionic Shimura curve; compare degrees with KRY's formula numerically.
refs: Kudla, Central derivatives of Eisenstein series and height pairings (Ann. Math. 1997)

title: Erdős–Kac jointly over levels: dependence of ω(4Cp+1) across C via shared small primes
connection: Level failures are dependent because 4Cp+1 and 4C′p+1 share small prime factors when C ≡ C′ mod q-structures. The joint distribution of (ω(4Cp+1))_C is a Kubilius-model question.
why: It quantifies how independent the per-level events are, the input any probabilistic or sieve approach needs.
first_step: Compute empirical correlations of 1[level C fails] across C ≤ 50 for p < 10⁷ and fit a Kubilius-type model.

title: Maynard–Tao: infinitely many primes p with many simultaneously prime 4Cp+1? (forced level failures; open whether it applies)
connection: If 4Cp + 1 is prime, its only divisors are 1 and itself (≡ 1 mod 4C), so level C fails. Maynard–Tao gives, for admissible tuples of linear forms, infinitely many n with ≥ m of them prime. If n can also be restricted to primes (check: Maynard's 'dense clusters' framework allows subsets such as the primes), this would give infinitely many primes p with ≥ m failed levels among C ≤ K.
why: It would be a PROVED statement about ES-hardness: arbitrarily many small levels fail infinitely often. It calibrates any proof that uses a bounded set of small levels, as a quantitative B1.
first_step: Check whether Maynard's 'Dense clusters of primes in subsets' (Compos. Math. 2016) applies with n ranging over primes and forms 4Cn + 1; state the resulting m(K).
refs: Maynard, Small gaps between primes (Ann. Math. 2015)
Maynard, Dense clusters of primes in subsets (Compos. Math. 2016)

title: Hilbert's irreducibility in the p-aspect: the word surface's fibres W_p as specialisations of a generic surface
connection: As p varies, W_p is a family over the p-line. Integral points on fibres correspond to integral points on the total space (t,u,v) with p = tuv − u − v, i.e. the total space is A³. ES₅ is surjectivity of a polynomial map ℤ³_{≥2} → primes with a sign condition.
why: 'Which values does a polynomial in several variables take at integer points with a sign restriction' is a native question about polynomial value sets (e.g. results on xyz + linear forms covering all large integers).
first_step: Look up results on value sets of polynomials of the shape xyz + ax + by + cz on integer boxes (e.g. 'every n is xyz + x + y' type theorems) and compare with Lorenzini's (W).

title: Chen switching for ES: Type I ↔ Type II role switch to upper-bound 'near misses'
connection: Chen bounded the bad P₃ contribution by sieving the switched set. ES: a 'near miss' at level C is a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a wrong class; switching d ↔ (4Cp+1)/d and C ↔ another parametrisation (Type I ↔ Type II) may convert hard lower bounds into upper bounds of a switched count.
why: Lower bound = (computable total) − (upper-bounded bad part) is the only robust way sieves get existence.
first_step: List all involutions/bijections between ES certificate sets (Type I/II, (★)↔b=1, level switching) and check whether any maps near-misses of one family to near-misses with a computable total in another.

title: Is ES parity-sensitive? A Selberg-parity test for certificate counts
connection: FI/Heath-Brown matter because sieves cannot distinguish parity of Ω. Test whether the ES certificate indicator correlates with λ(4Cp+1) or λ of the divisor: if certificate detection is 'parity-blind', sieve-theoretic approaches are not blocked by parity.
why: Clarifies whether parity-breaking technology is needed at all.
first_step: Compute Σ_C λ(d)·1[d certificate at level C] over all certificates for many p; compare with the total count.

title: Wieferich-type congruences forced on a hypothetical counterexample
connection: Mihăilescu showed a Catalan solution forces p^{q−1} ≡ 1 (mod q²) — strong congruences on the unknowns. ES: a counterexample p must be a square modulo every M for which bounded certificates cover the non-square classes (Mordell: mod 840). Push the list of forced congruences as far as possible and combine with the least-non-residue bound.
why: If 'no certificate with parameters ≤ L' forces (p/ℓ) = 1 for all ℓ ≤ L^c, Burgess (n(p) ≪ p^{0.152}) gives a contradiction for L^c > p^{0.152}.
first_step: For moduli M = 840·m, compute the residues uncovered by certificates with all parameters ≤ L; test whether they are exactly squares mod M and how L must grow with M.

title: Killing ramification: remove small-prime structure from a counterexample
connection: KW lower the level by passing through compatible systems. ES: a counterexample p is a square mod 840; transform the problem (via the e-slice or by passing to n = p·m for auxiliary m) to a 'less ramified' instance where certificates are easier, without losing the failure.
why: Speculative; but ES(pm) → ES(p) fails in general, so the transfer must use primitive certificates of pm (those not coming from m).
first_step: Count primitive (non-inherited) Type II solutions of 4/(pm) for small m and test whether they ever yield information about p's certificates.

title: Minimal counterexample via the e-slice: ES(p) from data of N = (p+e)/4 < p
connection: Four-colour and many combinatorial proofs consider a minimal counterexample. ES(p) ⟸ a property P(N, e) of the smaller integer N = (p+e)/4. Find a property Q(n), inherited along n ↦ (n + e)/4 for some e, such that Q(n) for all n < p implies Q(p) and Q(p) ⇒ ES(p).
why: A successful Q would make ES a consequence of verification (10¹⁸) + induction.
first_step: Data mining: for each p ≤ 10⁷, list e for which N_e carries a certificate and look for a hereditary property of N_e.

title: Graham's 77-theorem mechanism for ES-like partition problems
connection: Graham: if n is representable then so are 2n+2 and 2n+9, plus a finite check (78–333). The mechanism is affine closure maps. ES is closed under n → kn but no affine map n → an + b preserves solvability in general (it would be a Mordell-type identity). Determine all affine maps that preserve Type II solvability on some residue class.
why: Classifying affine closure maps tells exactly how far identity-based closure can go (Mordell–Schinzel-type limit).
first_step: Search a, b ≤ 100 for which ES-solutions of n map to solutions of an + b on a residue class, via the Type II parametrisation.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)

title: Tower of moduli with auxiliary primes (Shafarevich-style embedding problems)
connection: Shafarevich realised solvable groups by solving embedding problems step by step, choosing auxiliary primes to control local behaviour. ES: build a certificate as a sequence of lifts through moduli 4 → 8 → 24 → 840 → … with auxiliary prime factors of 4Cp+1 chosen at each step, keeping a global integer solution possible at each stage.
why: Gives a stepwise view of where integrality is lost; the final step (a genuine integer) is the crux.
first_step: Trace actual (★) certificates for hard primes: at which modulus in the tower does the certificate's structure become determined?
refs: Neukirch-Schmidt-Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Ch. IX

title: Residue-class case split with per-class constructions (Ringel–Youngs) — and its limit
connection: Ringel–Youngs proved the Heawood bound by 12 residue cases, each with its own construction family. ES: Mordell's identities do this for non-square classes mod 840; the square classes need infinitely many sub-cases. Measure how the number of needed per-class families grows with the modulus (cf. B1).
why: Quantifies the 'case explosion' and hence how far case-analysis approaches can go.
first_step: For M = 840·k, count the minimal number of polynomial certificate families needed to cover all non-square classes mod M; plot vs M.

title: Zeta-type packaging of Type I/II counts at p^k (T1 kills even k)
connection: Hasse–Davenport/Weil: point counts over all extensions assemble into a rational zeta function, so a few counts determine all. T1 gives f_{I,II}(p^{2k}) = 0 for odd p. Study f_{I,II}(p^{2k+1}) and the series Σ_k f(p^k) t^k: any rationality or recursion linking f(p³), f(p⁵), … to f(p) would make f(p) > 0 follow from large odd powers.
why: Odd powers of p may have solutions that do not come from p; a recursion would be a Hecke-type relation in the 'p-power direction'.
first_step: Compute f_I, f_II at p, p³, p⁵ for small primes p ≤ 200 and look for linear recurrences in k.

title: Affine-group encoding: (★) as a product-covering statement in Aff(ℤ/q)
connection: In small groups (affine group of F_q, order q(q−1)) the Gowers/Nikolov–Pyber thresholds are less demanding. The (★) condition (4uC − 1) | (p + u) can be read as an affine relation x ↦ 4uC·x − u evaluated mod divisors; look for a formulation as 'target ∈ A·B·C' in an affine group with sets of size ≈ q^{2/3}.
why: If an encoding into a small quasirandom-enough group exists, the 'one more factor' trick could cover every target mod q; integrality still needs a size argument.
first_step: Search encodings: map (u, C) ↦ affine maps mod q and check whether the product set of three natural sets covers Aff(F_q) for q ≤ 101.

title: Legendre-formula bookkeeping for Π_C(4Cp+1): which primes can make up the product?
connection: Sylvester–Schur works by bounding the contribution of small primes via Legendre's formula. For Π_{C≤K}(4Cp+1) the contribution of each prime q is explicit by CRT (q divides the terms with C ≡ c_q mod q). Compute the share of the product coming from primes q that could serve as single-prime certificates, versus the rest.
why: Makes the 'size argument' quantitative: if certificate-capable primes must contribute a definite share of log Π, one of them must divide some term in the right class.
first_step: Compute Σ_{q} (number of C ≤ K with q | 4Cp+1)·log q split by whether 4c_q | q+1-type conditions can hold.
refs: Erdos, J. London Math. Soc. 9 (1934) 282-288 (A theorem of Sylvester and Schur)

title: Class-equation divisibility: Φ_n(q)-type obstruction to 'no certificate'
connection: Witt's proof of Wedderburn: the class equation has all terms but one divisible by Φ_n(q), forcing a contradiction. For ES, write an exact counting identity for a quantity attached to p (e.g. Σ_C τ(4Cp+1) over a full period, or a divisor-class census over (ℤ/4C)*) as a sum over 'orbits' where all non-certificate terms are divisible by some cyclotomic-type number.
why: A divisibility contradiction needs no asymptotic analysis.
first_step: Look for counting identities over complete residue systems (C mod q) where certificate-free contributions have a forced common factor.

title: Primitive part of 4Cp+1 relative to smaller levels as a 'new divisor' source
connection: Zsigmondy isolates primes dividing a^n − 1 but no earlier term. For fixed p, call a prime factor q of 4Cp+1 'new' if q ∤ 4C′p+1 for C′ < C (equivalently c_q = C). New primes have c_q = C < q, and a new prime q is a single-prime certificate iff 4C | q + 1. Study the number of new primes at each level.
why: New-prime counts give an explicit, level-ordered supply of candidates with a clean certificate test.
first_step: For p ~ 10⁸ and C ≤ 10⁵ compute the new primes at each level and the frequency of 4C | q + 1.

title: Classify all 'transfer maps' between ES instances via the e-slice
connection: Graham's closure maps transfer representability from n to 2n+2, 2n+9. For ES, the e-slice transfers between p and N = (p+e)/4. Classify maps T: (N, e) ↦ (N′, e′) such that a certificate for (N, e) yields one for (N′, e′); a rich enough transfer system could connect every instance to verified ones.
why: Transfer systems are the engine of closure-type every-n proofs.
first_step: Search small linear maps (N, e) ↦ (aN + b, ce + d) preserving −1 ∈ Rat_e(N) on all data with N ≤ 10⁶.
refs: Graham, A theorem on partitions, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 3 (1963) 435-441 (77-theorem); see also Graham, Pacific J. Math. 10 (1960) 1221-1224 / OEIS A051882 (subagent dating conflict: check)

title: Two square degeneracies: algebraic factorisation (p + m²) vs reciprocity (ES Type I/II)
connection: p + m² degenerates at squares because n − m² = (a − m)(a + m) allows at most one representation (m = a − 1); T1 makes Type I/II fail at odd squares through a reciprocity cancellation. Compare: exceptional-set technology for p + m² is power-saving (H. Li 2003: E(X) ≪ X^0.982; verified), more advanced than ES's; can ES's T1 be rewritten as an algebraic factorisation in some model (e.g. 4Cm² + 1 or (p + e)/4 at squares)?
why: If T1 becomes algebraic in some coordinates, Hardy–Littlewood-type machinery for 'non-square n' transfers more directly.
first_step: At n = m², examine 4Cm² + 1 and (m² + e)/4 for algebraic factorisations that explain the absence of certificates (e.g. Sophie Germain-type identities).
refs: Hardy-Littlewood, Partitio Numerorum III, Acta Math. 44 (1923) (Conjecture H)

title: Exact characterisation of sub-route success sets (Brjuno-type)
connection: Yoccoz showed the Brjuno condition is exactly the linearisable set, turning 'almost every' into 'iff'. For ES sub-routes, seek the exact arithmetic characterisation of the success set (e.g. Type I ∪ II succeeds iff n is not an odd square and n ∉ finite list; (★) succeeds iff …), including a mechanism producing the failures.
why: An exact 'iff' is the strongest form of an every-type theorem and forces understanding of the failure mechanism.
first_step: For (★) and b=1, fit the failure sets ≤ 10¹⁰/10¹¹ to candidate closed-form conditions and look for a constructive mechanism that produces the failures (as Yoccoz constructed non-linearisable examples).

title: Brjuno-type sum as a certificate-difficulty index
connection: The Brjuno sum Σ log q_{n+1}/q_n measures cumulative small-divisor difficulty. Define an analogous additive difficulty index for p (e.g. Σ over small levels C of −log of the probability that level C fails given p's residues) and test whether ES certificate counts are governed by it.
why: A single scalar controlling difficulty would focus both proofs and adversarial searches.
first_step: Compute the index for primes ≤ 10⁹ and correlate with R(p), least certificate C and sub-route failures.

title: Absorbers from Mordell identities: reserve identity-covered structure to fix square classes
connection: Absorption reserves a structure that can repair any leftover. Mordell identities cover non-square classes; for a hard p, consider auxiliary integers N related to p (e.g. N_e = (p + e)/4, which may lie in easy classes) whose identity-certificates can be 'absorbed' into a certificate for p via the e-slice.
why: Transfers the power of identities (which fail only on square classes) to hard p through an auxiliary object.
first_step: For hard p, compute which N_e lie in identity-covered classes and whether their identity certificates translate into window certificates for p.

title: Polynomial congruence certificate: an identity in ℤ[X]/(X^r − 1, p) detecting ES
connection: AKS used a polynomial congruence that holds iff n is prime. Ask whether ES(p) has a characterisation by a polynomial identity modulo (X^r − 1, p) or modulo auxiliary moduli (e.g. a product over levels of polynomials whose evaluation detects certificates), testable deterministically.
why: Odd: algebraic characterisations sometimes admit clean counting proofs (as in AKS's group-size argument).
first_step: Construct the generating polynomial P_p(X) = Π_{C ≤ K} (1 − X^{[level C fails]}) style objects and look for algebraic relations they satisfy for all p.

title: Switching between the two cofactors of 4Cp + 1 and the two ES types
connection: Chen's switching replaces a hard count by a dual count where the roles of variables swap. In (★), 4Cp + 1 = (4uC − 1)(4BC − 1) is symmetric; the b=1 line uses p + 4d with a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4d). Find an explicit bijection/switch between near-certificates of one line and of the other, so that an upper bound for near-misses of one yields a lower bound for hits of the other.
why: Switching is the concrete mechanism behind complementary-route arguments.
first_step: Search for maps (u, B, C) ↦ (d, w) between (★) data and b=1 data for the same p, and test on hard primes.

title: Size-4 numerators are PROVED in F_q[T]: F_4[T] with A=T, F_2[T] with A=T²
connection: The two function-field analogues whose numerator has the same norm as 4 (|A| = 4: q=4,deg A=1 and q=2,deg A=2) are theorems (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES Thm 6.1, 6.3), proved by a FINITE congruence covering. Over Z a finite covering is impossible (Mordell square classes).
why: Pinning down exactly which Z-obstruction each FF proof dodges isolates the one ingredient Z lacks; it is the cleanest 'proved twin' of ES.
first_step: Tabulate for Thm 6.1/6.3 every covering family and mark which uses char-2 cancellation vs absence of the square-class obstruction (FUNCTIONFIELD_ES §6 'Why this exists over F₂').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Char-2 cancellation ↔ signed ES with a size-controlled negative term
connection: In char 2 two monic denominators of equal minimal degree cancel at ∞ (m = 2), which is what the F₂ identities exploit. Over Z the closest mechanism is 1/x − 1/x' with x' ≈ x, i.e. signed ES where the negative term is tiny.
why: If the F₂ identities lift to signed integer identities whose sign defect is confined to a small term, the remaining task is a 'sign repair' problem, which is a different and more concrete integer statement.
first_step: Lift the F₂[T] identity of Thm 6.1 coefficientwise to Z[T] (T ↦ integer), record which term goes negative, and measure its size relative to 4/n.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign-subgroup world: positivity = leading coefficient in a subgroup H ≤ F_q^*
connection: Monic (H = 1) is Hayes' choice; H = F_q^* is the trivial sign-free problem. Taking H = squares (index 2) mimics Z, whose sign group {±1} has index 2 in nothing but whose 'positive' half is index 2 in Z∖0.
why: Interpolating H shows whether hardness is controlled by the index of the cone; an index-2 cone FF problem might be the most faithful model of ℕ ⊂ Z.
first_step: Run the existing ffl_* search with leading coefficients restricted to squares for q = 3,5,7, deg P ≤ 8, and compare failure counts to the monic version.
refs: Hayes, 'Explicit class field theory in global function fields'
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Profinite sterile points: FF x* in ES₃(T²) vs non-square sterile profinite integers
connection: FF_STERILE_* constructs a profinite point x* of ES₃(T²) where every covering family fails (Haar-null set). Over Ẑ the odd squares are sterile for certificate lines; are there non-square sterile points in Ẑ?
why: If Ẑ has only square-type sterile points, ES reduces to squares-plus-growth; if it has others, they are new candidates for hard primes.
first_step: Mirror the FF construction in Ẑ: run the certificate-line covering tree mod 840·k and look for profinite branches avoiding all lines that are not square classes.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positivity at a finite place: cone = polynomials with constant term 1
connection: Replace 'monic' (sign at ∞) by 'X(0) = 1' (sign at the place T). This cone is multiplicatively closed but contains elements arbitrarily close to 1 T-adically, i.e. it is not discrete at its sign place.
why: The other_rings principle predicts collapse to a finite covering when the cone is not discrete at the sign place; checking it in a new world tests the principle.
first_step: Search for e with e = 1/U + 1/V, U,V in the cone, e ≡ 'class 3' modulo the analogue of 4 (T²?) — try q = 3,5 by brute force.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Genus-1 coordinate rings: ES over F_q[x,y]/(E) with sign at the point at infinity
connection: Drinfeld–Hayes rings with nontrivial class group: a 'prime' P generates a non-principal ideal in general, so 4/P is not even an element unless P is principal; ES becomes a statement about principal primes or ideal classes.
why: Separates the role of the class group (trivial for Z) from the role of the cone; if ES fails only in non-trivial class-group rings, class number one is part of the mechanism.
first_step: Pick an elliptic curve over F_3 with A = F_3[E∖O], enumerate principal primes of small degree and run the e-slice search with sign-normalized denominators.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sign groups at ∞: {±1} for Q versus F_q^* for monic F_q[T] in ray class groups mod m·∞
connection: With the sign at ∞, the ray class group mod m of F_q[T] is (F_q[T]/m)^* (Carlitz), and dropping the sign quotients by F_q^*; for Q the analogous groups are (Z/m)^* and (Z/m)^*/{±1}. (The narrow class groups themselves are trivial in both cases, since every ideal has a positive/monic generator.) So the 'sign part' of ray class groups has size 2 over Q and q − 1 over F_q[T].
why: ES-type certificate conditions are ray-class conditions; if FF hardness scales with the size of the sign part, Q (sign part of size 2) sits in the most constrained-sign regime.
first_step: Compute, for q = 3, 4, 5, 7, the failure rate of ES_q(T, P) at deg P = 6 against q − 1; fit.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over R[T] with lc > 0: the real-closed-coefficient world
connection: Over R[T] with positive leading coefficients there is no integrality of coefficients, so ES becomes a semialgebraic condition on the solution variety, like the q → ∞ limit but with an ordered constant field.
why: Separates 'ordered field at the sign place' from 'finiteness of the constant field'; if R[T]-ES is trivial, the Z difficulty is all integrality.
first_step: Check whether A/P = Σ 1/X_i with monic-real X_i always has solutions for deg A = 1 (dimension count + sign of leading terms).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: F_q[T] with q = p prime vs prime power: does F_4 behave like F_2 or like F_3?
connection: Thm 6.3 (F₄, A = T) and Thm 6.1 (F₂, A = T²) are both char 2. Comparing F₄ with F₉ (char 3) and F₂₅ isolates characteristic from field size.
why: Disentangles 'char 2 cancellation' from 'small q', which decides whether the |A| = 4 analogues are char artefacts.
first_step: Run the existing covering-tree search for q = 9, A = T (|A| = 9) and q = 3, A = T² to deg 8 and report covering success.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Polynomial ES over Z[T] for P of degree 2: 4/(T² + 1)
connection: Primes of the form T²+1 are ≡ 1 (mod 4) when T even. An identity for 4/(T²+1) over Z[T] with eventually positive denominators would cover them; T²+1 is never a square for T>0, so Mordell–Schinzel's square obstruction does not apply directly.
why: A quadratic-polynomial identity would be a non-linear certificate family; existence/non-existence probes whether the obstruction is genuinely about squares.
first_step: Search for 4/(T²+1) = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with X,Y,Z ∈ Z[T] of degree ≤ 4 (or with T in a fixed class mod M) via linear algebra on coefficients.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Polynomial ES at P = T² + T + 1, T⁴ + 1 and other never-square polynomials
connection: Generalizing the T²+1 test: for each irreducible quadratic/quartic f that is never a square and has values ≡ 1 mod 4, ask for a Z[T] identity. Mordell–Schinzel's obstruction is pointwise at square values, which f avoids.
why: A positive find would be a genuine new infinite certificate family for primes of a polynomial shape.
first_step: Run the same coefficient search as for T²+1 on a list of ten such f; note obstructions at fixed T mod M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Exponential-polynomial identities: denominators in Z[T, 2^T] or Z[T, p^T]
connection: Allow denominators that are exponential polynomials in an auxiliary parameter (e.g. identities in which a variable exponent k enters as 2^k or 3^k). Such families are not quasi-polynomial in n and escape Mordell–Schinzel's formal framework.
why: Growing families with exponential parameters (power ladders) are one of the few certificate shapes outside B1; the identity world Z[T, a^T] is their natural home.
first_step: Formalize POWER_LADDER_ES families as identities over Z[T, 2^T] and ask whether any covers a full square class mod 840 for all T.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Q(T) with denominators in Z[T] but positivity 'for T in an interval' (semi-algebraic cone)
connection: Instead of eventual positivity (lc > 0), require denominators positive on [0, ∞) or on an interval. This cone is not multiplicatively a valuation cone and sits between Z[T]-lc and genuine pointwise positivity.
why: Mordell–Schinzel uses positivity on infinitely many integer points; different positivity notions show exactly how much positivity the obstruction needs.
first_step: Check whether T1 at squares already kills identities whose denominators are positive only for T in a residue class mod M.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: FF Thm 6.3 search technique (covering trees) on Z with growing modulus
connection: The computer-assisted FF proofs used a covering tree whose leaves are congruence classes with identities. Over Z the same tree never closes (squares), but its growth rate measures the 'certificate deficit'.
why: The FF/Z comparison of tree growth quantifies the gap; a sub-exponential growth over Z would suggest a growing-family proof is plausible.
first_step: Run the FF covering-tree code verbatim on Z (moduli 840·k) to depth 6 and record the number of open leaves per depth vs the FF case.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: F_q[T] with q → ∞ AND deg P → ∞ jointly: the critical scaling deg P ≈ c·q
connection: Thm 2.1 (fails, q→∞ fixed degree) and Thm 5.3 (density-0 failures, fixed q) bound a phase diagram; along deg P ≍ f(q) there is a critical curve.
why: The critical curve is the FF version of 'expected number of solutions ≍ log² p'; its exact location in FF predicts how close Z is to the threshold.
first_step: Compute failure proportions on a grid q ∈ {3,5,7,9,11,13}, deg P ∈ {3..7} and fit the 50%-failure curve.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Artin–Schreier identities in char p: the 'Frobenius twist' certificate family
connection: In char p, X ↦ X^p is additive, so identities like 1/X^p − ... interact with Frobenius; e.g. (P+1)^p = P^p + 1. Certificate families using P^p are unique to char p.
why: A Frobenius-twist family that covers an FF class unreachable otherwise shows a char-p-only mechanism; over Z its only shadow is Fermat's little theorem congruences (power ladders mod p).
first_step: Search char-3 identities where a denominator is (P + c)^3 or P^3 + c and see whether they cover classes the linear families miss.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q[T] with the extra condition 'distinct denominators' — equivalent or not?
connection: Over Z, distinctness is (believed/known) harmless for n > 2. In F_q[T] char 3, the trivial 3/P = 1/P+1/P+1/P shows repeats matter; with distinctness the char-3 numerator-3 case becomes non-trivial.
why: A distinctness-sensitive FF world is a new problem whose behaviour in char 3 could mimic Z with numerator 4.
first_step: Check whether 'ES_3(T, P) with distinct monic denominators' fails anywhere for deg P ≤ 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over F_q[T][1/T] (S-integers in FF) — analogue of Z[1/3]
connection: Inverting a prime T in F_q[T] gives units T^k; the other_rings Lemma 3.1 then supplies universal divisors e | 1 + T^k with e in the 'class 3' analogue, collapsing ES.
why: Confirms the cone-discreteness principle in FF and quantifies how many units are needed (smallest k).
first_step: Find smallest k with a divisor of 1 + T^k in the needed class mod A for q = 3, A = T²+1.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field ES with A irreducible vs A reducible (4 = 2·2 is reducible)
connection: 4 = 2² over Z; FF analogues with A = T² (reducible, proved over F₂) vs A irreducible of degree 2. If the reducible case is systematically easier, ES's numerator being a prime square is relevant.
why: Points at whether 4 = 2² structure (square of the dyadic prime) is used by any Z mechanism.
first_step: For q = 3, compare failure sets for A = T² vs A = T² + 1 (irreducible) at deg P ≤ 8.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Smooth-numerator relaxation is trivial: 4/n = 2/n + 1/n + 1/n
connection: Allowing numerators that are S-units (S-integer denominators) trivializes ES already with numerators (3, 3, 1) — the depth-1 identity. Even 4/n = 2/n + 1/n + 1/n works, so the least smoothness bound is ≤ 2; the relaxation is uninformative unless the number of non-unit numerators is restricted (see ν(p) item).
why: Filter: prevents a wasted computation and redirects to the 'one non-unit numerator' world, which is weighted ES (1,1,ℓ).
first_step: None beyond recording; pursue the ν(p) / weighted (1,1,ℓ) items.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Totally positive ES over arbitrary number fields K with an infinite unit group
connection: Generalize Prop 3.3: if K has a totally positive unit η and a prime ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4) (rational, inert or split suitably) with η ≡ −1 (mod some prime above ℓ), positive ES holds for rational n. Conjecture: true for every K with unit rank ≥ 1 and a totally positive unit of infinite order.
why: Would show the Z difficulty is exactly 'unit rank 0 + discreteness', i.e. Q and imaginary quadratic fields are the only hard worlds among number fields.
first_step: Try K = Q(√3) (N(ε) = +1) and a cubic field with mixed-sign units; search η^j ≡ −1 mod ℓ numerically (other_rings evidence covers D = 3, 6, 7).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Semiring cones Z_{≥0}[α] for α a Pisot or Salem number
connection: For α Pisot, Z_{≥0}[α] is discrete at the dominant place while conjugates shrink — like β-expansions. ES over these cones links to β-numeration (Pisot finiteness property F).
why: If ES-type statements over Z_{≥0}[α] relate to finiteness properties of β-expansions, there is a dynamical-systems literature to borrow.
first_step: Check the Frougny–Solomyak finiteness property (F) and test a numerator-4 ES in Z_{≥0}[golden ratio].
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Erdős–Straus for Gaussian integers / over ℤ[i]: does the analogue hold and does its proof (if any) use something ES lacks?
connection: ES over ℤ[i]: 4/α = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with Gaussian integers; the extra units and the splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 (p = ππ̄) change the problem: for p ≡ 1 mod 4, 4/p = (4/π)(1/π̄) — the hard primes split! The question 4/π for a Gaussian prime π of norm p.
why: Over ℤ[i] the analogue might be easier (more structure) or provably different; comparing sheds light on what ℤ lacks. Repo may have this (git grep Gaussian).
first_step: git grep -il 'gaussian integer' -- '*.md'; if absent, compute solutions of 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z over ℤ[i] for norm(π) ≤ 10⁴ with |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ N(π)² and see whether every π has one.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0067] Brute force: for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) ≤ 10^4, find Gaussian-cone solutions using π-divisors; look for a uniform identity.
refs: BRAINSTORM/ (Gaussian normalisation noted in z52 synthesis)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive-definite integer matrices: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹
connection: In Sym_k(Z) with the positive-definite cone, diagonal solutions are k copies of ES; non-diagonal X allow far more freedom. For k = 2, is (4/n) I always a sum of three inverses of positive-definite integral matrices?
why: A proof via non-diagonal matrices would be a 'matrix ES' theorem; projecting back (e.g. by the (1,1) entry x₂₂/det X) gives 4/n as a sum of three fractions with structured numerators.
first_step: Search k = 2: enumerate positive-definite integral X with small entries and check whether (4/n)I − X⁻¹ − Y⁻¹ is the inverse of an integral PD matrix, for n = p ≤ 1000.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0361] Search for solutions with X, Y, Z ∈ M₂(ℤ) symmetric positive definite for A = diag(p, 1) or companion matrices; record whether integer-matrix ES is always trivially solvable.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Group rings Z[C_m] with cone N[C_m]: ES in a ring with zero divisors
connection: Z[C_m] ≅ order in ∏ Q(ζ_d); the cone N[C_m] (non-negative coefficients) is multiplicatively closed and discrete in the trivial-character coordinate but not in others.
why: Combines several cyclotomic components with one positive coordinate; tests whether a single 'augmentation' coordinate carrying positivity suffices for hardness.
first_step: For m = 2 (Z[C_2] ≅ order in Q × Q), determine positive ES for n·1 and compare with ES over Z × Z.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Units of Z[1/2]: 4 becomes a unit and ES is trivial — the dyadic place carries the problem
connection: If 2 ∈ S the numerator 4 is a unit and ES collapses. Together with the Z[1/p] item: the obstruction is spread over the dyadic place and the place p.
why: Suggests a two-place reformulation: ES as a gluing problem between a 2-adic and a p-adic condition with an archimedean constraint.
first_step: Write ES as 'there exist local solutions at 2, p, ∞ with a common global lift of bounded height' and check it against STRONG_APPROX_ES.md.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ring of algebraic integers Z-bar with totally positive cone: ES trivially true?
connection: In the ring of all algebraic integers, every element has square roots etc.; with a totally positive cone, the unit-sum mechanism has infinitely many units, so ES should collapse.
why: A sanity endpoint of the classification (infinite-degree world).
first_step: Note as corollary of Prop 3.3: Z-bar ⊃ Z[√2]; any rational n has a totally positive solution. Record.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix ES over M₂(Z) with the cone of matrices with positive entries
connection: Matrices with positive entries form a multiplicatively closed cone discrete at ∞ (entries ≥ 1). Inverses are rational; ES: (4/n)·I = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-entry, invertible over Q.
why: This cone links ES to SL₂(N)-type monoids and continued fractions (the repo's SL₂ words form); it might reproduce ES exactly or relax it.
first_step: Check: does a solution with positive-entry X, Y, Z force a solution of ES? Compute small cases n = 5, 13, 17.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field–number-field bridge: Q(√D) ↔ F_q(T)(√D(T)) real quadratic function fields
connection: Real quadratic function fields (D of even degree with square leading coefficient) have units (Pell polynomial solutions); the unit-sum mechanism applies there too.
why: Shows the unit mechanism is uniform across global fields and identifies Pell-polynomial units as the FF counterpart of η.
first_step: Take q = 3, D = T² + 1, find the fundamental unit (Pell polynomial) and test the mechanism for monic P.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dual numbers Z[ε]/(ε²): the tangent-space ES
connection: 4/(n + mε) = Σ 1/(x_i + a_i ε) ⇔ ES for n plus the linear condition Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/n². The a_i are free integers, so the dual-number world asks which ES solutions have a solvable linear tangent condition.
why: Tangent conditions measure how rigid ES solutions are; a 'deformation' world might connect to counting solutions with multiplicities.
first_step: For p ≤ 10^4 and each solution compute gcd conditions for Σ a_i/x_i² = 4m/p² to be solvable for all m.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ring of formal power series Z[[T]]: ES for 4/(n + T) trivial by Hensel-type lifting?
connection: Over Z[[T]] with 'positivity' of the constant term, 4/(n + T) = Σ 1/X_i requires ES for n at T = 0 plus solvable higher-order equations; higher orders are linear in the corrections.
why: If every ES solution lifts formally, the variety is smooth at integer points along this deformation — a structural fact about the solution variety.
first_step: Check the Jacobian rank of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) at known integer solutions (is the surface smooth there?).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Tropical/valuative cone over F_q((1/T)): ES 'at ∞' is a leading-coefficient problem
connection: Over the completion F_q((1/T)) with monic cone, ES is the leading-coefficient equation (Lemma 1.1); over R the analogue is just inequality x > n/4. Comparing the completed worlds isolates what is local at the sign place.
why: Shows that in FF the sign place gives a discrete leading-coefficient constraint while over R it gives only an inequality — a structural difference to keep in mind for dictionaries.
first_step: Write both local problems and their solution sets; record as a dictionary entry.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings
